issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette: John is a 46-year-old married European-American graphic designer who recently sought help for symptoms related to his traumatic experience. The event began one evening when he was walking home from work and found himself at the center of an intense police operation. Surrounded by police officers in full gear, John felt utterly helpless as they forcibly detained him without explanation. The abruptness and perceived injustice of his treatment left a profound impact on him. Since then, John has experienced persistent intrusive thoughts about the traumatic event. He often finds himself vividly recalling the moment when he was surrounded by uniformed officers. Even seemingly mundane sights-like visible injuries or wounds on others-can trigger intense flashbacks that leave him feeling overwhelmed and emotionally drained. The mere presence of authority figures, particularly police officers, now evokes a sense of dread and anxiety. In an effort to cope with these overwhelming feelings, John has developed several maladaptive strategies. He spends long hours engrossed in his phone, playing games or browsing the internet as a way to distract himself from his intrusive thoughts. Avoiding social interactions and keeping his mind constantly occupied have become habitual responses to mitigate the emotional pain. However, these coping mechanisms have come at a cost. John has grown increasingly isolated, pushing away friends and family who worry about him but cannot understand why he avoids social gatherings or stays holed up in his room for hours on end. His work as a graphic designer has also suffered; deadlines are missed, and projects go unfinished due to his constant preoccupation with distractions. John's body is perpetually on high alert. Even when he knows he is in safe environments, like at home or within familiar surroundings, he cannot relax. He meticulously plans escape routes whenever he enters any space, no matter how benign it might seem. This hypervigilance has left him feeling constantly tense and ready to react to perceived dangers, making even simple daily activities exhausting. Recalling the traumatic event is particularly difficult for John. When the memory resurfaces, it often comes without warning and leaves him overwhelmed with emotion, unable to continue his day. He struggles to articulate what happened, finding himself unable to complete stories about the trauma or explain his feelings clearly to others. This frustration has only reinforced his sense of isolation. John's negative appraisals have profoundly affected his outlook on life. The incident has left him feeling as though everything in his life lacks meaning and that he is stuck with a fractured existence that cannot be repaired. He feels deeply wronged by the lack of accountability or justice for what happened to him, further fueling his sense of injustice. The accumulation of these symptoms eventually became too much to bear silently. John's wife had grown increasingly concerned about his behavior and urged him to seek help, recognizing that he needed support beyond their relationship. His current state is one of deep fear that the trauma will continue to define his life without any relief in sight. However, there is also a glimmer of hope; he is seeking therapy with the belief that it might offer some respite from the overwhelming burden of his experiences. John's journey towards healing is marked by a mix of dread and cautious optimism. He is acutely aware of how much the trauma has impacted every aspect of his life, but there remains an underlying desire to reclaim a sense of meaning and purpose in his daily existence.
